paragraphs: The paper studies the Kernel Fisher Discriminant, a classifier whose behavior the authors describe in terms of maximizing an average margin. A margin measures separation associated with classification. Expressing this objective as a mathematical programming problem provides a different way to understand the algorithm and a direct starting point for modifying it.

The authors use that formulation to develop a sparse version of Kernel Fisher Discriminant. They also give a shared probabilistic interpretation of the original and sparse methods. This connects the optimization view—what quantity the classifier tries to improve—with a statistical view of what the model represents. The paper further identifies relationships with Support Vector Machines and Relevance Vector Machines.

These connections lead the authors to outline a kernel regression technique based on the same approach, extending the discussion from classification to predicting numerical values. Simulations support the usefulness of the proposed framework. The contribution therefore combines an algorithmic modification with a common interpretation that helps relate several kernel learning methods.
neurips-2000-a-mathematical-programming-.tldr: An optimization formulation of Kernel Fisher Discriminant yields a sparse variant and connects it to other probabilistic kernel methods.

paragraphs: The paper adapts the support vector approach to clustering, where the task is to group data without supplied class labels. It maps observations into a high-dimensional feature space and uses support vectors to define an enclosing sphere. Viewed back in the original data space, that sphere produces closed boundaries, with observations inside each boundary forming a cluster.

The Gaussian kernel's width controls how tightly these boundaries follow the data. Decreasing the width can split a boundary into separate contours, revealing finer groupings. Because separation follows valleys in the underlying probability distribution, clusters can have arbitrary geometric shapes. The method therefore provides a way to identify groups whose outlines are more complicated than simple compact regions.

A soft margin parameter lets the method accommodate outliers and obtain smoother boundaries. Together, kernel width and the soft margin parameter provide controls for exploring data structure. The authors investigate how results depend on these choices and apply the algorithm to several datasets, making parameter behavior a central part of the study.
neurips-2000-a-support-vector-method-for.tldr: Support vector clustering turns a sphere in feature space into flexible cluster boundaries controlled by kernel width and outlier tolerance.

paragraphs: The paper examines concept learning as an active process: people can seek information through questions and experiments instead of only receiving observations. The central issue is how they choose what to ask next. A question's usefulness depends on what a learner currently believes and how much its possible answers could clarify the concept being learned.

The authors use expected information gain as a framework for examining those choices. In plain language, this evaluates how much uncertainty a question is expected to remove before its answer is known. It provides a principled way to compare possible questions while accounting for the learner's current beliefs, rather than judging a question only after seeing its answer.

The paper reports an exploratory experiment on people's information gathering in a concept task and analyzes participants' questions through this framework. Its contribution is to bring observed question choices into contact with a formal account of informative experimentation. The abstract describes this analysis without asserting that participants consistently choose the questions with the greatest expected information gain.
neurips-2000-active-inference-in-concept.tldr: An exploratory concept-learning experiment examines people's questions through the expected information those questions could provide.

paragraphs: APRICODD addresses planning in Markov decision processes, where a system must choose actions across many possible states. Dynamic programming uses value functions to describe how desirable those states are and derive a policy for choosing actions. The paper seeks to make this computation practical when exact intermediate value functions demand too much time and memory.

The method represents value functions with algebraic decision diagrams. Its key approximation replaces the numerical values at diagram terminals with ranges of values. This reduces the sizes of the intermediate representations created during value iteration. The approximation thus acts on the objects that the planning computation repeatedly constructs, directly targeting their storage and processing requirements.

The authors report near-optimal value functions and policies with substantially lower time and space requirements than exact dynamic programming. They demonstrate the approach on a class of large problems containing up to 34 billion states and compare the approximate results with optimal value functions. These comparisons connect the computational savings to the quality of the resulting plans.
neurips-2000-apricodd-approximate-policy.tldr: APRICODD compresses intermediate value functions with decision diagrams to obtain near-optimal plans at much lower computational cost.

paragraphs: The paper asks how quickly a large-margin linear classifier's expected error can decrease as more training examples become available. Its setting is a linearly separable problem, meaning a linear boundary can separate the classes. Existing results, under appropriate assumptions, describe error approaching zero at a rate proportional to the inverse of the training sample size.

Such convergence descriptions usually involve the margin and the largest norm of an input example. The authors argue that these geometric quantities do not tell the whole story. They introduce the robustness of the input distribution as another important factor in characterizing how quickly expected misclassification error declines. This shifts attention toward the distribution generating the observations.

Using this robustness concept, the paper shows that expected error may decrease exponentially with training sample size for a large-margin separable problem. Exponential decay can be much faster than an inverse-sample-size rate. The result is a possibility tied to the distributional analysis, rather than a claim that every separable dataset or large-margin classifier enjoys exponential convergence.
neurips-2000-convergence-of-large-margin.tldr: Distributional robustness can help explain why expected error may decrease exponentially in large-margin separable linear classification.

paragraphs: The paper considers an apparent mismatch between a reinforcement-learning account of dopamine activity and some observed responses. In the temporal-difference account, dopamine neurons provide a broadly shared learning error signal. Substantial evidence supports this interpretation, but activity in response to some non-rewarding stimuli seems anomalous if the signal is understood only through that role.

The authors propose that dopamine cells carry information about reward bonuses alongside the conventional error signal. They discuss exploration bonuses and shaping bonuses that do not distort the underlying task objective. These additional signals give the model a way to interpret activity that may be useful for learning and behavior even when a stimulus supplies no direct reward.

The proposed extension links dopamine's effects on attention and psychomotor activity to the computational problem of guiding exploration. On this account, the same neural system could help determine where behavior should seek useful experience as well as support learning from rewards. The paper presents this as an explanation for the anomalies, preserving its status as a suggested additional role for dopamine.
neurips-2000-dopamine-bonuses-a1c9e506ae.tldr: The paper proposes that dopamine carries exploration and shaping bonuses alongside reward-learning errors, helping explain responses to non-rewarding stimuli.

paragraphs: The paper studies learning linear decision boundaries in the agnostic setting, without prior assumptions about the distribution producing examples. The corresponding sample problem is to find the boundary that agrees best with the observed labels. Even approximating this best agreement within a certain constant factor is computationally hard, motivating a different definition of learning success.

The authors introduce a margin-based success criterion. It compares the returned classifier's agreement with that of competing boundaries after disregarding training points within a specified margin of the competing separating plane. This changes the target against which an algorithm is evaluated. It allows near-boundary points to be excluded from the comparison instead of demanding the original best-agreement objective.

For every fixed positive margin, the authors prove that an efficient polynomial-time algorithm meeting this criterion exists. They also establish a complementary barrier: unless P equals NP, no algorithm can be polynomial in both sample size and inverse margin while satisfying the criterion for every positive margin. Efficiency at a fixed margin therefore does not imply uniformly efficient behavior as margins shrink.
neurips-2000-efficient-learning-of-linea.tldr: A margin-based success criterion permits efficient linear learning for each fixed positive margin, with a hardness barrier as the margin varies.

paragraphs: The paper extends sparse coding from individual natural images to sequences of images. Sparse coding seeks a representation in which relatively few components are active while information about the input is preserved. Earlier work on still scenes produced features resembling certain visual neurons; this study asks what properties emerge when the input includes movement over time.

The proposed algorithm learns from natural video sequences. Its learned basis elements represent motion in particular directions and at particular speeds, resembling the receptive fields of movement-sensitive cells in visual cortical areas. This connects an information-preserving learning objective with motion-selective representations, showing that such properties can emerge through learning from moving imagery.

Timing also carries information in the resulting representation. The timing of neuronal activity encodes the phase of movement, so precise spike timing is important to what the model represents. The contribution therefore concerns both which motion patterns learned units respond to and when they respond. The stated resemblance to biological cells supports a modeling connection without establishing that the brain uses this exact algorithm.
neurips-2000-emergence-of-movement-sensi.tldr: Learning an information-preserving sparse code from natural video produces motion-selective features whose activity timing encodes movement phase.

paragraphs: The paper analyzes Gallager error-correcting codes through a statistical-physics framework. Its starting point is a mean-field approximation that changes the geometry of the model while retaining important interactions between sites. This creates a simplified description intended to preserve relationships that matter for understanding the code and its decoding behavior.

Within that description, the probability propagation decoding algorithm emerges as the search for an extremum of an appropriate free-energy function. This gives a common mathematical interpretation to decoding updates and the physical model. Instead of treating the algorithm as a separate procedure, the analysis relates its behavior to the structure of the free energy.

The authors find a thermodynamic phase transition that coincides with information-theoretic upper bounds. They also use the free-energy landscape to explain practical code performance. These are linked but distinct contributions: one concerns a transition associated with theoretical limits, while the other concerns how the decoding process behaves in practice. The framework connects both questions through the same approximate physical model.
neurips-2000-error-correcting-codes-on-a.tldr: A mean-field analysis connects Gallager-code decoding to free-energy optimization and relates a phase transition to information-theoretic bounds.

paragraphs: The paper combines a neuromorphic chip with a learning algorithm to control the gait of a four-legged robot. A small network of coupled oscillators generates changing voltages that drive the leg motors. By coordinating the relative timing of these signals, the chip plays a role inspired by the proposed function of spinal central pattern generators.

The output voltages depend on adjustable input parameters. For an idealized circuit, the relationship between parameters and outputs can be calculated analytically. Real hardware departs from that ideal because of transistor mismatch and offsets, so the analytical relationship is only approximate. The practical problem is therefore to tune the actual chip to produce the desired behavior.

An unsupervised support vector learning algorithm performs this tuning automatically. Given a description of the desired output, the system learns from unlabeled examples how to set the chip's parameters. The contribution joins a compact rhythmic controller with a learned adjustment mechanism, allowing the robot to account for hardware behavior when selecting the settings needed for a requested motor pattern.
neurips-2000-four-legged-walking-gait-co.tldr: An unsupervised support vector algorithm tunes a neuromorphic oscillator chip to produce desired four-legged robot motor behavior.

paragraphs: The paper develops a unified approach to adaptive transform coding for compression. Transform coders are often assembled by choosing a transform and then separately arranging bit allocation and quantization. The authors instead begin with a probabilistic model so that the coding procedure can be derived from a common foundation rather than assembled from loosely connected choices.

Their starting model is a mixture of constrained Gaussian mixtures with latent variables. From it, they derive a coding algorithm that is a constrained form of the generalized Lloyd algorithm for vector quantizer design. The derivation also produces a new transform basis explicitly optimized for coding. This makes the choice of representation part of the compression objective itself.

Image compression experiments report signal-to-noise ratio improvements of up to 3 dB over global transform coding and 0.5 to 2 dB over other adaptive transform coders. These are reported experimental gains, with the largest global-transform improvement expressed as an upper observed gain. The results support coordinating transform design and coding decisions within the proposed probabilistic framework.
neurips-2000-from-mixtures-of-mixtures-t.tldr: A probabilistic mixture model yields a coding-optimized transform algorithm that improves image compression signal-to-noise ratio in experiments.

paragraphs: Gaussianization tackles high-dimensional density estimation: learning how probability is distributed across observations with many coordinates. The paper attributes much of the difficulty to the curse of dimensionality and proposes exploiting independence structure in the data. Its aim is to make the modeling problem more manageable by progressively changing the representation of the observations.

Each iteration has two stages. First, the data is transformed into coordinates that are as weakly dependent as possible. Then each coordinate is individually transformed toward a Gaussian distribution using a one-dimensional technique. Repeating these operations combines a treatment of relationships between coordinates with simpler transformations of their individual distributions. The authors establish weak convergence for this iterative procedure.

The paper reports sharper density estimation than traditional kernel and radial basis function methods. It also interprets Gaussianization as an efficient approach to nonlinear independent component analysis and high-dimensional projection pursuit. These connections explain why the procedure is useful beyond making individual variables Gaussian: it aims to organize the joint distribution so that its dependence structure becomes easier to handle.
neurips-2000-gaussianization-51b25046a2.tldr: Gaussianization alternates dependence-reducing coordinate transformations with one-dimensional Gaussianization to estimate high-dimensional densities.

paragraphs: The paper studies generative modeling for data whose values cannot be negative. Under constraints matching first- and second-order statistics, the relevant maximum-entropy model is a Nonnegative Boltzmann Distribution. The nonnegativity restriction therefore affects the appropriate model family, making the support of the observations a substantive part of the statistical formulation.

Learning this model requires computing expectations under its distribution, which becomes difficult at practical problem sizes. The abstract identifies a tradeoff: Markov chain Monte Carlo methods are computationally costly, while naive mean-field approximations have low fidelity. The paper addresses this calculation with a second-order mean-field approximation derived using a high-temperature expansion.

The approximation is tested on three settings: a two-dimensional distribution with two modes, a high-dimensional translationally invariant distribution, and a generative model of handwritten digits. These tests examine the theory across different distributional structures and scales. The central contribution is a more developed approximation for the expectations needed in learning, with the stated experiments providing applications rather than a quantified claim of superiority.
neurips-2000-high-temperature-expansions.tldr: A high-temperature expansion provides a second-order mean-field approximation for learning Nonnegative Boltzmann models.

paragraphs: The paper implements homeostasis in a silicon integrate-and-fire neuron. Here, homeostasis means adjusting activity over seconds or minutes so that the neuron returns to its spontaneous firing rate after a sustained perturbation. The focus is on slow adaptation of the neuron's behavior, allowing it to recover a baseline level of activity despite a lasting change.

Two mechanisms provide this adaptation. One monitors presynaptic activity and changes the synaptic weight according to the incoming spike rate. The other changes a synaptic threshold according to the neuron's own activity. Prolonged decreases in activity lower the threshold, while prolonged increases raise it, providing an adjustment that opposes the sustained change in firing.

Both mechanisms use floating-gate technology, and the reported results come from measurements of a chip fabricated in a 2-micrometer CMOS process. This makes the contribution a physical implementation of adaptive neural regulation. The two schemes demonstrate ways to base that regulation on either incoming activity or the output activity of the silicon neuron itself.
neurips-2000-homeostasis-in-a-silicon-in.tldr: A silicon neuron uses floating-gate adaptations of synaptic weight or threshold to recover its baseline firing rate after sustained perturbations.

paragraphs: The paper examines how known properties of a target function can be built into a learning model. The setting assumes that the function is non-decreasing in two inputs and convex in one. These are structural constraints on how predictions may change as inputs vary, giving the learner information beyond the observed training values.

The authors propose a function family resembling multilayer neural networks that satisfies these properties by construction. They also establish a universal approximation property for continuous functions with the specified and other stated properties. This matters because incorporating constraints should still leave the model flexible enough to approximate the relevant class of functions, rather than forcing one narrow functional shape.

The application is regression for call-option prices. Experiments show improved price prediction when the proposed function classes incorporate the prior constraints. The findings support using known monotonicity and curvature properties as part of model architecture in this setting. The approximation result concerns functions within the constrained class, while the empirical result concerns the option-pricing task studied.
neurips-2000-incorporating-second-order-.tldr: Neural-network-like function classes that enforce known monotonicity and convexity improve call-option price regression in experiments.

paragraphs: The paper presents a support vector machine training procedure that processes one training vector at a time. Its central concern is how to incorporate a new example while preserving the optimization conditions associated with previously seen examples. This gives online learning a precise relationship to the constraints defining the support vector solution.

The update proceeds through gradual increments that retain the Kuhn–Tucker conditions on earlier training data. Each step is computed analytically. These conditions describe the relationship between the solution and its optimization constraints, so maintaining them is more specific than simply making a small change to the classifier's parameters after receiving a new observation.

The incremental process is reversible, allowing examples to be removed through decremental unlearning. The authors use this capability to evaluate leave-one-out generalization performance exactly and efficiently: each example can be assessed with its contribution removed from training. They also interpret removal geometrically in feature space, connecting the effect of individual observations with the relationship between data geometry and generalization.
neurips-2000-incremental-and-decremental.tldr: A reversible SVM update preserves optimization conditions while adding examples and enables efficient exact leave-one-out evaluation by removing them.

paragraphs: The paper seeks a scalable way to construct Bayes point classifiers. The Bayes point is the center of mass of the version space: the set of linear classifiers consistent with the training data. It expresses the Bayesian idea of averaging across compatible classifiers, but an earlier sampling algorithm required memory and computation growing quadratically with training sample size.

The authors propose a method based on the simple perceptron learning algorithm to overcome that computational drawback. The method extends readily to multiple classes, and its computational effort can be adjusted through the number of posterior samples. This makes the amount of sampling a practical control over the work spent constructing the classifier.

Experiments on MNIST show performance competitive with support vector machines in the reported comparison. The paper also examines rejecting predictions using approximate posterior probabilities. It reports 0.1% generalization error at a 10% rejection rate. That figure describes selective prediction, where some test points are declined, and should be interpreted together with the fraction of cases rejected.
neurips-2000-large-scale-bayes-point-mac.tldr: A perceptron-based method scales Bayes point learning and achieves competitive MNIST performance, with further error reductions when uncertain predictions are rejected.

paragraphs: The paper learns relationships between sound and video so that one signal can help interpret the other. This is difficult because the signals have many dimensions, can be sampled at different rates, and have complicated statistical dependencies. Simple parametric joint models may be tractable, but the authors argue that they cannot capture the relationships needed here.

The approach first projects the observations into a low-dimensional subspace chosen to retain as much information as possible. It then estimates the joint distribution using a nonparametric density model. These stages work together: the projection makes density estimation more manageable, while the flexible estimator models stochastic relationships between the auditory and visual signals.

The learned distributions support processing in both directions. On synthetic and real signals, the authors demonstrate locating the speaking face in video using audio, and enhancing a particular speaker's audio after selecting that person visually. The contribution is a shared statistical representation that allows information from either modality to guide a task involving the other.
neurips-2000-learning-joint-statistical-.tldr: A learned nonparametric audio-visual distribution supports locating speakers in video and enhancing the audio of a visually selected speaker.

paragraphs: The paper develops upper bounds for statistical learning calculations that are otherwise difficult to handle directly. Jensen's inequality is often used to obtain tractable lower bounds in settings such as latent-variable learning and Bayesian inference. Those bounds can simplify integration or optimization, but some learning objectives, particularly discriminative ones, also require bounds from above.

The authors derive and prove an efficient analytic inequality that supplies variational upper bounds. Its stated scope is latent-variable mixtures of exponential-family distributions, a class covering many statistical models. The result provides an additional mathematical tool for this family; the title's reversal refers to obtaining the needed upper-bound direction within that setting.

The paper discusses applications to maximum conditional likelihood, large-margin discriminative models, and conditional Bayesian inference. It also presents convergence, efficiency, and prediction results. These applications show why the bound matters operationally: a manageable upper bound can make objectives involving hidden variables more accessible to learning procedures. The contribution combines a proved inequality with investigations of its use in several conditional and discriminative modeling tasks.
neurips-2000-on-reversing-jensen-s-inequ.tldr: A proved analytic inequality supplies variational upper bounds for latent-variable exponential-family mixtures and supports conditional and discriminative learning.

paragraphs: The paper uses products of experts to learn generative models of handwritten digits. These models combine probabilistic experts and discover stochastic binary features that represent nonlinear image structure. A separate model is learned for each digit class, allowing a test image to be assessed through the scores assigned by the different class models.

Recognition improves by organizing each class's models into a hierarchy. Each level has one hidden layer, and the next level learns from the hidden-unit activities produced by the previously trained level. Every level supplies its own unnormalized log-probability score. With three levels for each of ten digits, an image generates thirty scores describing its compatibility with the learned models.

A supervised logistic classification network, trained on separate data, combines those scores into a digit prediction. The resulting system is reported as comparable with contemporary leading discriminative methods on MNIST. The finding supports the usefulness of the learned high-dimensional generative representations, with recognition achieved by combining their class-specific, multilevel scores in a final supervised classifier.
neurips-2000-recognizing-hand-written-di.tldr: Hierarchical, class-specific products of experts provide scores that a supervised classifier combines for competitive handwritten-digit recognition.

paragraphs: The paper investigates nonlinear support vector machines for the visual sex-classification task defined in its face dataset. The inputs are very small face images: thumbnails measuring 21 by 12 pixels, processed from 1,755 images in the FERET database. This focuses the study on how much useful classification information remains in low-resolution facial imagery.

The authors compare support vector machines with several established pattern classifiers. These include linear and quadratic classifiers, Fisher linear discriminant, and nearest-neighbor methods, along with radial basis function classifiers and large ensembles of radial basis function networks. The comparison tests the nonlinear support vector approach against multiple alternative ways of classifying the same kind of visual input.

The reported support vector machine error is 3.4%, and the abstract states that its performance exceeds the compared methods. It also describes the result as the best reported in the open literature at the time of the paper. The finding is an empirical result for the studied image-classification setting, showing strong performance despite the small size of the input images.
neurips-2000-sex-with-support-vector-mac.tldr: Nonlinear SVMs achieve a reported 3.4% error on sex classification from low-resolution FERET face images, outperforming the compared classifiers.

paragraphs: The paper proposes a sparse, greedy approximation to the maximum a posteriori estimate in Gaussian process regression. Its aim is to improve how computation scales with the number of training examples. The approximation uses a size parameter n that is much smaller than the full sample size m, making sparsity central to the computational savings.

The stated computational requirement is O(n²m), with O(nm) storage. Prediction costs O(n), while computing confidence bounds costs O(nm). These separate costs clarify where the smaller representation helps: producing a prediction depends on n, whereas the reported confidence-bound calculation still depends on the training sample size as well. Keeping n small is therefore important to the proposed scaling behavior.

The authors also provide a computable stopping criterion and bounds on approximation error. These address how to decide when the greedy procedure has done enough work and how to characterize the resulting approximation. Applications to large-scale problems accompany the analysis, connecting the method's computational motivation with its use beyond small training sets.
neurips-2000-sparse-greedy-gaussian-proc.tldr: A sparse greedy Gaussian process approximation improves scaling and includes a stopping criterion and approximation-error bounds.

paragraphs: The paper studies how spike-timing-dependent learning shapes networks with oscillating activity. Synaptic changes depend on activity before and after a connection, together with a timing kernel that specifies the effect of a postsynaptic spike occurring at a given delay after a presynaptic spike. The learning rule therefore incorporates the temporal relationship between connected neurons.

The resulting synaptic matrices have an outer-product structure, with oscillating patterns represented by complex vectors. In a simple model, different parts of the timing kernel have distinct effects. Its even component strengthens the resonant response to a learned stimulus by reducing effective damping. Its odd component determines the oscillation frequency.

This separates two consequences of temporal learning: how strongly a learned pattern resonates and how quickly the network oscillates. The authors relate the model to the olfactory cortex and hippocampus, discussing their presumed roles in associative memory and input representation. These biological connections frame the model's relevance, while the stated division between damping and frequency is a result within the simple model analyzed.
neurips-2000-spike-timing-dependent-lear.tldr: In a simple oscillatory-network model, different components of spike-timing-dependent learning control learned resonance strength and oscillation frequency.

paragraphs: The paper models how people solve anagrams using a connectionist constraint-satisfaction system. The model draws on statistical patterns in English spelling to help arrange letters into a solution. Its broader aim is to explain how distributed, subsymbolic processing can interact with more explicit symbolic representations during a task associated with higher cognition.

The key mechanism extracts an approximate symbolic representation from the network's subsymbolic state. That representation consists of partial orderings of letters, capturing some information about their arrangement without requiring a complete solution. The extracted information is then injected back into the model to assist further processing. Symbolic structure therefore becomes an intermediate resource within the ongoing solution process.

The authors demonstrate a computational benefit from this extraction-and-reinjection mechanism. They also account for experimental findings about anagram difficulty associated with the spelling structure of both the scrambled string and the target word. Discussion connects the mechanism to conscious mental processing and working memory, giving the computational model a proposed relationship to psychological processes involved in solving anagrams.
neurips-2000-the-interplay-of-symbolic-a.tldr: An anagram-solving network benefits from extracting partial symbolic letter orderings and feeding them back into its distributed computation.

paragraphs: The paper explores reinforcement learning in large factored Markov decision processes, where representing every state-action value in a table can become impractical. It approximates each Q-value with the free energy of a product of experts network. This gives the learner a parameterized representation of action values that can be used when an explicit table grows too large.

Network parameters are updated online through a modified SARSA algorithm. The updates reduce inconsistency between the values of consecutive state-action pairs. To choose an action, the method fixes the current state and uses Gibbs sampling to sample actions from the network according to its current value estimates. The network thus participates in both value representation and action selection.

Tests use a cooperative multi-agent task. For small instances, the product of experts approach performs comparably to table-based Q-learning. It also continues to perform well on instances too large for the table representation. The findings support this representation on the studied task, linking its practical value to the growth of the state-action space.
neurips-2000-using-free-energies-to-repr.tldr: A product of experts network represents Q-values through free energy and performs well on a cooperative task beyond practical table sizes.
